blocks.p: In the grey hour after, on the floor of his apartment with the curtains still drawn against an Obon dawn, Rei did the only thing he knew how to do with a horror. He made it a document. He listed the grieving. The man from Sumida whom the circle had lightened. The widow. The mother. Kanna-sensei's thirty-five soothed faces. The man from the Ōedo line and the daughter whose name Rei had said out loud. And the crying courier whose name was Kaito, whose grief had apparently been the largest unattended account in the ward. Beside each name he drew which demon needed them, and how.

The pattern that came up made his hands go still on the pen. They needed the same people. The Healer needed the mourners gentle and intact, so the membrane could be drawn down slowly through their willing grief. Kishin needed the mourners raw and breaking, so the membrane would tear. The hunt was not two predators chasing each other across the city. It was two physicians fighting over the same dozen patients, and every move either one made to win ran straight through a living room where someone was trying to grieve in peace.

Which means, he wrote, and then sat looking at the words a long time before he let himself finish the sentence. Which means there is no clean side. To starve Kishin's flood he must keep the mourners soothed. That meant letting the Healer keep soothing them. So the price of stopping the loud catastrophe was feeding the gentle one a little more every night. And to deny his brother his quiet door he must let the griefs go raw, which handed the flood its fuel. The wiring was built so that any cut in one line charged the other. Rei had read enough poisonings to know the shape of a trap that uses its victim's own care as the mechanism. The more he loved the living, the more he served one demon. The more he loved the dead, the more he served the other. And the only person in the whole diagram placed to see this and refuse it was sitting on a cold floor at dawn with ink on the side of his hand.

He thought about calling it in. The CVD had a word for what to do with a room like the Far-Shore Circle. Gin's playbook said address, and Gin's playbook said that addressing was Reintegration's work. Rei had seen the word in the CVD's own brochures and never asked what it meant. He took Gin's book down from the shelf and found the chapter. It was the one place in the whole archive where his brother stopped writing to a reader and wrote to him.

blocks.cap: A reintegration cell in the suppression wing

doc.title: Gin's book. Reintegration. The word they use
lines: What happens to a medium who loses control, breaks the law, or is simply found before they register. The CVD calls it rehabilitation. I have stood in the rooms. The word is doing a great deal of work.
I have put this chapter off for a year. Writing it makes it mine to have known.

If you are reading this, you were an unregistered medium yourself for most of your life, and you did not know it, because I made sure the registry never looked at you. This chapter is the reason I did that.

There are three ways a medium comes to the CVD's attention without choosing to. Loss of control. A Correction Event, a crisis read that produces a casualty, a possession that completes in public, a child whose passive ability outruns their capacity to hold it. Criminality. And the most common and least forgiven, simply being found.

The after-action reports say recovered, condition stable. A frightened Arbiter-rank sensitive cornered in a stairwell is not a person to the team. It is a Scale event with a stability number attached.
Then there are two outcomes, and everyone inside says the same two words. Integrate, or contain.
Integration can save people. I have watched it. It is also not a choice. Integration is conscription. The alternative to signing is not freedom. It is the second word.

The suppression cell. A cube of metal about sixteen feet on a side. Five faces are a double lattice of silver and iron bars set into poured resin of sulfur, gunpowder and ground shards of holy bone, with the suppression glyphs printed on the outside where the occupant can never reach them. The sixth face is bars and a tray slot. Inside, everything is white. A bed, a desk, a chair, a shelf of books. The light is always on. They keep you medicated, because a mind that comes apart thins the membrane. For a practitioner it is not like being locked in a room. It is like being locked out of your own hands.

And while they are held, they are trained. The facilities are on no map I was cleared to see. What I have, from three operatives who would only talk obliquely and one who talked because he could not stop, is this. The aim is obedience that has survived being broken. The name history already has for places like that is camps.

The ones with operational value are placed under a higher-ranked medium, a Master in the older language, and used. As a decoy, drawing entity attention from a team that matters more. As bait, walked into a thin spot because something there will come for them. As a battery, a read, a held door. The report says asset attrition.
Madness is not a risk in that system. It is a schedule. I have met four of the reintegrated. The stillness the cells leave reads as a place where something used to be.
The cruelty is not a betrayal of the system's values. It is the system's values, fully costed.
I do not regret the hiding. I regret that I could only hide one person. I ran out of time before I could even finish writing down why.
If you join them, join them knowing this is in the building with you. Make them say it to your face, in plain words, with the lights on. Then decide.

One number, the only one I could confirm. Of the practitioners recorded entering containment in the Kita region over the six years I worked it, the share ever recorded leaving by any door at all is under one in three. The file does not say what happened to the others. (G.U.)

doc.title: Stuck inside the back cover of the chapter
lines: Visited the suppression wing once. Did not sleep. Will not go back unless ordered. G.U.

blocks.p: Rei read it twice. Then he sat with his back against the bed for a long time and let the floor of his life rearrange itself. All the years of Gin saying keep your head down, keep it quiet, it's nothing, you're just tired. All the forms Gin had never let him fill in. His brother had stood between him and that white room every single day and never told him it was there. And now his brother was the one with his hand on the forms. I sign them now, you know.
He crossed out the word address on his page. He could not hand thirty-five grieving people and a hollowed courier to a building that ran this with the same hands as its good people.

He thought of Kurosawa, who read bodies, who had told him once that the cause of death is rarely where the cruelty is. He thought of the seam he had found in Kishin's sermon, the living, left off the books. And slowly he realised it was the seam in the Healer's plan too. Both demons had done their arithmetic on the dead. Neither had costed the living, except as supply. The place neither of them was looking was not a person or an address. It was the whole category of the breathing, treated by both reasonable catastrophes as the medium and never the matter. If there was another way through, it was somewhere in that blind spot. In doing something for the grieving that was neither soothing them into batteries nor breaking them into floods. The harder thing, the thing demons had no use for. Helping them actually mourn, and be done, and walk out of the diagram entirely.

He went back through Gin's book looking for anything his brother had written about that harder thing, and found it in a place he had not expected. It was a short section near the end, headed The quieter cases. Gin is not the only one carrying something, it began, in Gin's own voice about himself. The city is full of quieter cases. People with a thing riding them, a thing feeding on them, or a dead friend they cannot or will not release. Each one turns on the question the whole book turns on. Do you treat the afflicted as a case to close, or a person to keep? The win is rarely an exorcism and usually a kindness.
Two of the files were marked with a red pencil tick, as if Gin had meant to come back to them.

blocks.cap: Kuroki Tatsuo, and the thing that climbs with him

doc.title: Kuroki Tatsuo. The Climb. Possession in progress
lines: Yakuza lieutenant, Shinjuku family. Fifty-one. A discreet house in Mejiro, a family man at home. Most nights at Kogane or a private room. His line. I can find anyone in this city. The finding is free. The owing is not.
The most dangerous case in the book, because nobody is looking at it.

An Ambition-register demon, unnamed, attached itself to him years ago and has been, in effect, helping him. Removing his rivals in ways no rival could manage. Sharpening his judgement. Giving him a luck he reads as his own. It does not want to harm him. It wants him to rise, because the higher a host climbs, the more ambition and fear pool around him, and that is what it eats.

It is not fully in. It rides at the edges, a whisper that feels like instinct. If it completes the crossing, and a host this fed is close, the city gains an Arbiter-grade demon wearing a powerful man with an army.

Tells. Rivals vanish too cleanly. He never loses, and has not in years. The room drops a degree when he is pleased. He has begun finishing other people's sentences. He sleeps four hours and wakes sharper.
Reachable only before the full crossing. He is proud and intelligent and keeps his family clean. Shown what rides him, he might fight it. Or he refuses to believe and becomes a slow-burn enemy.
His soldier Wada Sho is the soft way in. Twenty-nine, a share-flat in Ōkubo, frightened more often than he shows. (G.U.)

blocks.cap: Aizawa Yuto, and the hunger latched onto him

doc.title: Aizawa Yuto. The Hole That Eats. Attachment, not possession
lines: Twenty-two. An heir, addicted. A family-owned flat in Hiroo he rarely sleeps in sober. Most nights at Vault, the expensive bars, the after-hours rooms. His line. My family has money for everything except the thing I actually need. Funny, right?

Not a possession. A feeder. A low Hunger-register thing latched onto him at his lowest and has been widening the emptiness ever since, because the emptiness is its meal. The addiction is half chemistry and half the thing deepening the hole so he keeps reaching for the next thing to fill it. Nothing fills it. That is the point.

Tells. He never feels full of anything. Drink, drugs, company. The air near him goes faintly cold and hungry. People leave his table vaguely depleted. Objects of comfort lose their savour around him. Thinner every month, and the doctors find nothing.
Leo the host has felt the cold off him and not known why.
Clearing the feeder is necessary and not the win. The human wound stays. A freshly cleared Aizawa is a frightened young addict who now has to feel everything. A rescue, not an exorcism. (G.U.)

blocks.p: A rescue, not an exorcism. Rei underlined it twice. Gin had known. Gin had written down, in his own hand, the thing neither demon could see. Clearing the hunger was not enough. Somebody had to stay afterwards and help the person feel everything.

Kaito came to him the next night, because of course he did. Rei was the table, and the table is where both of them set things down. He woke at 3:47. He always woke at 3:47 now, the kitchen's hour following him like a debt. The courier was sitting on the fire escape on the other side of the glass, knees drawn up, looking out at Kita, where the membrane held its hundred-year breath. He did not try the window. In the host's body he was almost peaceful, the flood gone quiet the way floods are quiet between rains.

"He's getting closer to catching me," the thing in Kaito said through the glass, conversationally. Rei understood it meant his brother, the Healer, the gentle hunt closing. "He'll fold this mouth back into the schedule if he does. Make the grief a tap. Or file the boy into one of his white rooms. I'd rather you stopped me than him."

It took Rei a moment to hear what had actually been said. Then it landed. It was asking him to be the one who defeated its catastrophe, rather than his brother. To a thing that loved the truth, being stopped by the one who found the seam was less of an insult than being managed by the liar.

Rei sat on his own side of the glass. He did not open the window and he did not look away. He asked the question he had been carrying since the basement. What would actually let the held dead rest? Not flood and not tap. Rest. The thing both the ruin and his brother's mercy only pretended to offer.

For a long moment the courier's face did something the flood had not let it do. Something that belonged to the young man and not to what spoke through him. A flicker of a person who used to deliver other people's parcels through this exact ward at this exact hour, and who knew from the inside what it was to carry something that was never yours to its door.

"Rites," Kaito said, so quietly the glass barely carried it. "Real ones. Names said out loud by someone who means it. Like you did in the basement. That's what they were owed. That's what nobody had the time for. He offers to file them and it offers to free them, and neither of them is offering them their names."

Then the flood came back up over his eyes like water over a stone, and he was the mouth again, and the moment was gone. But Rei had it now, written on the inside of him where the registers could not soften it.

When the courier left, he went the way grief goes, without any sound. Rei sat at the window in the kitchen's stolen hour with the other way through finally clear and impossible in its size. A hundred years of the unnamed dead, owed their names by a city with nine million living mouths and not one institution willing to spend the time.

Not one institution. He got up and found the sheet Tanizaki had given him, folded in three, in Gin's handwriting. Do not read it today, Tanizaki had said. You will know the day you need it. Rei unfolded it under the kitchen light.

doc.title: Outside the doctrine. The houses that still do the old work
lines: Pak Sun-ja. Mudang. Fifty-five. Above a Korean restaurant in Shin-Ōkubo, a shrine room behind a curtain. Performs gut for the community, for healing, for mourning, for the restless dead. She negotiates rather than banishes. She treats an entity as a guest with a grievance and hears it out. For spirits anchored to grief she outperforms exorcism more often than the Division will admit in writing. Slower than a banishment. It lasts. By introduction only. She decides whether to see you, and payment is the least of it. Her words. The dead are not gone, only unquiet. I can ask them. Sometimes they answer. I watched her talk a thing down in an afternoon that I had decided could only be fought.

Rev. Egami Jakū. Shingon priest. Fifty-nine. The old temple in Kita-ku with the working graveyard, the same one the grave-earth comes from. Funerals publicly, the inner rites for those who truly need them. A priest who will sit with a spirit and grieve it rather than file it. A true esoteric exorcism, which the Directorate cannot replicate, is a transaction with the unseen that takes something real from the one who performs it. He has done three and considers each a wound still healing. He will not be anyone's weapon. Prove the cause is worthy, not just urgent. Approach as a mourner, not a client. They taught me that some things do not need to be defeated, only seen all the way out.

Father Anselm Mabuchi. Catholic priest. Sixty-one. An old parish a few streets from the CVD building. The institution walks past it daily. The side door, after the last Mass, by appointment through someone he already trusts. He will ask hard questions first, and he is right to. The Roman rite names the thing and commands it. Absolute on some registers, useless and dangerous on others. Good for a demon that answers to authority and name. Bring him the right case or none at all. He has hidden people the bureau wanted, and he would do it again. Rome has its rite, he says. I have my conscience. When they disagree, the conscience wins.

Master Lin Wei. Taoist temple master. Sixty-three. The temple in the Chinese quarter, the old lineages out in Yokohama's Chinatown. Fú talismans, paper that binds the dead. Buy incense first. Then we talk. The respect is not optional. It is the method. Disrespect the temple and the talismans simply do not take. At full trust he draws a true fú for one specific entity. I keep one of their talismans in my kit and cannot fully explain why it works. It works.

Baba Adewale. Babalawo of the Ifá tradition. Sixty-four. A flat that doubles as a community house, candles always lit. Casts the cowries before he answers and pours a little for the orisha first. A system of divination the CVD does not know exists, and he has handled crossings it never heard of. If an entity answers to nothing you were taught, it may answer to someone whose grandmother knew its kind by another name. You go as a guest asking to learn. You are brought, or you do not go. His word opens Adé's back room. I learned once, badly, not to treat a living faith as a tool in my kit. I deserved it. (G.U.)

blocks.p: Five houses. Five people who still said names out loud and meant them. Not one of them had a desk at the CVD. Rei could not say a hundred years of names. He did not know if anyone could. But he had seen the courier remember being a person. And he had seen his brother, in the basement, glance at his face out of an old reflex of love that the Healer had not bothered to erase. At the bottom of the worst week of his life, with both catastrophes leaning on him like weather, he thought the blind spot both demons shared might also be the one place his brother was still in there.

Neither of them had costed the living. But his brother, before he was the Healer's coat, had costed exactly one living person above everything else. He had hidden him from the registry every day for years. His name was Rei, and he was sitting at the window, awake at 3:47, with a list of five names in his hand, refusing to be only the table.
